screens.title: Controller-Based Interactions and Haptics
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how controllers make XR interactions feel direct and meaningful. We’ll start by configuring hand controllers so they can touch and grab objects, using the XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable components to make virtual objects respond like real ones. Next you’ll learn to wire controller buttons through Unity’s Input System so scripts can react to actions like firing a projectile. Then we’ll add haptics — short tactile impulses sent to the controller — so users feel collisions, grabs, and weapon fire. Along the way I’ll point out common setup mistakes, how to tune intensity and duration, and why thoughtful haptic design matters for comfort and clarity. By the end you should be able to set up a throwable object, trigger haptic pulses on grab and release, and design distinct vibration patterns that communicate different events. Think about a sphere that snaps to your hand, vibrates when you pick it up, and kicks when you fire it — that concrete behavior is our target. Ready to explore the key topics and build a simple throwable demo?

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Controller-Based Interactions
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Controller-Based Interactions and Haptics

Configure XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable, wire input actions, and add meaningful haptic feedback to make XR interactions feel tactile and safe.

16:9 HD Classroom
In this lesson

Set up direct grab interactions, detect button actions, and design haptic cues that match events.

Why it matters: tactile cues improve clarity and immersion while correct physics prevent surprising behavior.
Coming up

A hands-on throwable object demo: grab, throw, and fire with haptic pulses on grab, release, and fire.

Explore Key Topics
Direct Interaction
Use XR Direct Interactor plus colliders and rigidbodies to make objects grabbable and follow the controller.
Input Actions
Define actions in an Input Action Asset to map buttons to game events like FireProjectile.
Haptics
SendHapticImpulse lets you vary intensity and duration to communicate different events safely.
Visual Concept
Hand controller + sphere
Hand collider reaches object, XRGrabInteractable responds and follows.
Attach Transform
Defines how the object aligns to the hand. Use a child empty object if hold position is awkward.
Haptic Example
On grab: light pulse. On release: stronger pulse. On fire: short, strong impulse using SendHapticImpulse.
Next step
Follow the hands-on activity to add an XRGrabInteractable sphere, wire a FireProjectile action, and trigger haptics for clear feedback.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will build. First, you will configure XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable so virtual objects respond to a user's hand presence and follow the controller when grabbed. That includes colliders, rigidbodies, and the Attach Transform concept. Second, you will implement button-press detection with Unity’s Input System and the XRI action-based controller model. You’ll learn how to create an action in an Input Action Asset, bind it to a controller control, and subscribe to events in C#. Third, you will integrate basic haptic feedback by calling SendHapticImpulse through the XR controller's input device and learn sensible defaults for intensity and duration. Finally, you will learn a pattern for wiring actions to gameplay code so grab, release, and custom actions like firing a projectile trigger both game logic and haptic responses. Each objective ties to the hands-on demo: a throwable sphere that vibrates on grab, release, and when you fire a projectile. Keep these goals in mind as we walk through setup, code, and haptic design.

screens.title: XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable
screens.narratorSegment: Direct interaction models physical touch and grabbing in XR. The XR Direct Interactor is attached to a hand representation — typically a small trigger collider around the controller position plus a kinematic rigidbody — and it detects overlap with objects that have XRGrabInteractable. The XRGrabInteractable makes an object grabbable and controls how it follows the interactor. A key setting is Attach Transform: by placing an empty child at the desired holding point and assigning it, you define exactly where the object aligns with the hand. A concrete example: give each hand a sphere collider set as Is Trigger and a kinematic Rigidbody, add XR Direct Interactor to that hand, then add XRGrabInteractable to a Sphere in the scene. When you reach the collider into the sphere, the object becomes selectable and will follow the controller. A common misconception is thinking colliders alone are enough — without a properly configured Rigidbody on either the interactor or the interactable, physics-based detection or motion will fail. The takeaway is to treat the interactor, colliders, and rigidbodies as a small system: each must be present and correctly configured for natural grabbing behavior.

keyIdea.text: XR Direct Interactor detects hand overlap; XR Grab Interactable makes objects follow the interactor and uses Attach Transform for correct alignment.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Direct Interaction
Definition

XR Direct Interactor

A component attached to a hand representation that uses a trigger collider to detect and select grabbable objects.

Quick checklist
  • 1. Hand has Sphere Collider (Is Trigger) and Rigidbody (Is Kinematic).
  • 2. Add XR Direct Interactor to hand controller gameobject.
  • 3. Add Collider + Rigidbody + XRGrabInteractable to the grabbable object.
Key Takeaway

All three pieces — interactor, colliders, and rigidbodies — must be configured for reliable direct grabbing.

Illustration
Hand controller
Sphere collider (trigger), kinematic Rigidbody, XR Direct Interactor component attached to this GameObject.
Grabbable object
Collider + Rigidbody (non-kinematic for physics throws) + XRGrabInteractable component.
Example scenario
Place a sphere at (0,1.2,1), attach XRGrabInteractable and a Rigidbody with Is Kinematic unchecked so you can pick it up and throw it normally.
Common mistake: missing Rigidbody or collider not set to trigger; either prevents the interactor from selecting the object.

screens.title: Configuring Hand Controllers for Direct Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring the hand controllers is a small sequence of precise steps that ensure reliable interaction. Start by locating your LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller as children of XR Origin. Add a Sphere Collider to each, and set Is Trigger so the collider does overlap checks rather than physical collisions. Then add a Rigidbody and mark it Is Kinematic on the hand object; this allows the interactor to participate in physics queries without being pushed by scene forces. Next, attach the XR Direct Interactor component to the same hand GameObject so the toolkit will treat the trigger collider as an interaction zone. For objects you want to pick up, add a Collider and a Rigidbody. Decide whether the object should be physics-driven when thrown — if so, leave Is Kinematic unchecked. Finally, add XRGrabInteractable to the object. A concrete example: for a throwable sphere, set its Rigidbody Is Kinematic to false so it reacts to forces, then assign XRGrabInteractable. Test in Play Mode: when the hand's trigger collider overlaps the sphere, it should become selectable. If not, check the Rigidbody presence and trigger setting. This step-by-step flow reduces common misconfiguration errors and produces predictable grab behavior.

keyIdea.text: Hand setup sequence: Sphere Collider (Is Trigger) → Rigidbody (Is Kinematic) → XR Direct Interactor; Object: Collider → Rigidbody (physics as needed) → XR Grab Interactable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Controller Setup
Procedure
  1. Add Sphere Collider to each hand. Set Is Trigger.
  2. Add Rigidbody to hand and set Is Kinematic.
  3. Add XR Direct Interactor component to hand object.
  4. For grabbable object, add Collider + Rigidbody; set Is Kinematic based on whether it should be physics-driven.
  5. Add XRGrabInteractable to the object and tune Attach Transform if needed.
Pro tip

If the object snaps oddly, create an empty child at the desired grip position and assign it to Attach Transform.

Illustrated checks
Trigger collider
Should be set to Is Trigger so it detects overlap events instead of causing physics collisions that push objects away.
Rigidbody settings
Hand rigidbodies are kinematic. Interactable rigidbodies can be dynamic for throws or kinematic for static follows.
Behavior test
In Play Mode, reach in with the controller and confirm the object becomes selectable without jitter.
Common failure
If grabs fail, check that the action map is enabled and colliders are correctly layered and not blocked by geometry.

screens.title: XRGrabInteractable Details & Attach Transform
screens.narratorSegment: XRGrabInteractable controls how an object is selected and how it moves when attached to a controller. A central property is Attach Transform: by default the object may attach at its root which often misaligns with natural grips. Create an empty GameObject as a child of the grabbable, position it where the virtual hand should hold the item, and assign that child to Attach Transform. This gives you precise control over rotation and offset so the object appears correctly held. Another important behavior is whether the object follows with physics or simply matches the controller transform. For physically realistic throws, leave the object's Rigidbody non-kinematic so physics apply when released; XRGrabInteractable supports picking up physics objects and applying release velocity. For static snapping behavior, mark the Rigidbody kinematic and the object will follow the interactor transform more directly. An example: to make a mug feel natural in the hand, create the grip attach point near the handle and adjust rotation so the mug's opening faces up. A common misconception is assuming Attach Transform only affects visuals — it actually defines the transform used by the interactor to position and rotate the object while held, and getting it wrong leads to awkward snaps and poor UX.

keyIdea.title: Attach Transform
keyIdea.text: Use a child Attach Transform to define the hold point and decide Rigidbody kinematic state to control physical or snap-follow behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Attach Transform
How it works

Attach Transform and Rigidbody behavior

Attach Transform specifies the exact point and rotation used when the object is held. Rigidbody kinematic setting decides whether the object is physics-driven on release or simply follows the interactor.

Grip alignment
Create an empty child at the desired grip and assign it to Attach Transform to prevent misaligned snaps.
Physics vs Snap
Dynamic rigidbodies allow realistic throwing; kinematic rigidbodies produce direct transform following.
Concrete example
Mug grip
Position the Attach Transform near the mug handle and rotate the child so the mug rests naturally in the virtual hand.
Test steps
  • Assign Attach Transform child and run Play Mode.
  • Grab and inspect alignment; adjust the child until the hold is natural.
  • If throwing is desired, ensure Rigidbody Is Kinematic is unchecked so release velocity applies.

screens.title: Common Grabbing Mistakes & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When a grab does not work or the object snaps strangely, two issues are usually responsible: collider/rigidbody misconfiguration and incorrect Attach Transform settings. First, check colliders. The hand collider should be set to Is Trigger. If it is not, it will generate physical collisions and can push objects away. Both the interactor and the interactable must have colliders that overlap. Second, verify Rigidbodies. The hand rigidbody is typically kinematic so it is not affected by physics forces, while the interactable's Rigidbody may be dynamic for throws. A missing Rigidbody on either side can prevent selection or cause jerky motion. Third, check Attach Transform: if the object snaps to an unexpected position, assign a child object positioned at the desired grip. Another frequent problem is disabled action maps or unbound actions preventing controller input events: when scripts look for an action that is not enabled, callbacks never fire. Finally, layering and collision matrix settings can hide overlaps. The practical fix is a short checklist: confirm trigger colliders, confirm rigidbodies, confirm Attach Transform, ensure action maps are enabled, and test in Play Mode. This focused troubleshooting flow resolves most common grabbing failures quickly.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Common Mistakes
Problem
Grab fails or snaps awkwardly.
Collider issues
Ensure the hand collider is set to Is Trigger and that it overlaps the object's collider when attempting to select.
Rigidbody issues
Confirm both objects have Rigidbodies with appropriate Is Kinematic settings for the desired behavior.
Attach Transform
If snap is awkward, supply a child Attach Transform positioned where the hand should grip.
Checks and fixes
Quick fix list
  1. Confirm hand collider Is Trigger.
  2. Confirm both objects have Rigidbody components.
  3. Adjust Attach Transform to correct grip offset.
  4. Ensure action maps are enabled for input events.
Common misconception
Believing collider presence alone is sufficient. Without matching Rigidbody and proper trigger settings, selection will fail.

screens.title: Button Press Detection with Input Action Asset
screens.narratorSegment: Detecting button presses with the action-based model begins in the Input Action Asset. Open your XRI Default Input Actions or create a custom Input Action Asset. Inside the asset create or locate the action map for the hand you want to use, for example XRI RightHand. Add a new action named FireProjectile with Action Type set to Button and add a binding to the right-hand trigger control, such as the triggerPressed control for the XR controller. This abstract action can now be referenced by scripts without hardcoding device paths. In C#, you find the action map by name on the InputActionAsset and then FindAction to get the specific action. Enable the action map and subscribe to the action's performed event. A concrete example is adding a FireProjectile action bound to the right trigger and in Start() enabling the map and subscribing to performed. A common pitfall is forgetting to enable the action map, which results in callbacks never firing. Another is using a wrong action path; always test bindings in Play Mode. The result is a clean, decoupled way to respond to controller buttons across devices and form factors.

keyIdea.text: Define actions in an Input Action Asset, bind them to controller controls, and subscribe to performed events in C# after enabling the action map.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Input Actions
Setup

Create a FireProjectile action in the XRI RightHand action map and bind it to the right-hand trigger. Set Action Type to Button.

Why this matters
Actions provide device-agnostic inputs, letting you map gameplay logic to an abstract action rather than a specific button path.
Common mistake: forgetting to enable the action map at runtime so performed callbacks never execute.
Example code
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

public class SimpleActionListener : MonoBehaviour
{
  [SerializeField] private InputActionAsset inputActionAsset;
  private InputAction fireProjectileAction;

  void Start()
  {
    var rightMap = inputActionAsset.FindActionMap("XRI RightHand");
    fireProjectileAction = rightMap.FindAction("FireProjectile");
    rightMap.Enable();
    fireProjectileAction.performed += ctx => OnFireProjectile();
  }

  void OnDestroy()
  {
    if (fireProjectileAction != null) fireProjectileAction.performed -= ctx => OnFireProjectile();
  }

  private void OnFireProjectile()
  {
    Debug.Log("Fire Projectile action performed!");
  }
}
This pattern finds the action, enables its map, and subscribes to the performed callback to run gameplay logic when the button is pressed.

screens.title: Wiring Input Actions to Controller Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Once your Input Action Asset contains the desired action, your script should locate the action map and action, enable the map, and then subscribe to the action events. The example in the lesson shows finding the XRI RightHand action map and then calling FindAction to get FireProjectile. After enabling the map, subscribe to performed to run your logic when the button is pressed. In the handler you can instantiate gameplay objects such as a projectile and then call a haptic helper to provide tactile feedback. Importantly, unsubscribe in OnDestroy to avoid dangling callbacks. Also, check that the XRController reference used to send haptics is assigned and that its inputDevice is valid before calling SendHapticImpulse. A concrete example: call TriggerHapticFeedback(0.5f, 0.2f) after instantiating a projectile. A common error is not checking controller. inputDevice. isValid which will cause SendHapticImpulse to silently do nothing; always guard your haptic call with a validity check. The end result is a clean wiring where button presses spawn projectiles and immediately send a haptic pulse so the player receives both visual and tactile confirmation. Wiring Input Actions to Controller Scripts means enable the action map, subscribe to performed, perform gameplay logic, and call a guarded haptic helper that checks device validity.. In practical terms, subscribe to actions and trigger haptics from your script. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Action Wiring
Pattern
  1. Find action map on the InputActionAsset.
  2. Find the action by name and enable the map.
  3. Subscribe to performed and implement gameplay response.
  4. Use a TriggerHaptic helper that verifies the controller device before sending impulses.
  5. Unsubscribe in OnDestroy to clean up.
Misconception

Forgetting to unsubscribe or to enable the action map are the most common runtime mistakes and both are easy to miss during development.

private void OnFireProjectile(InputAction.CallbackContext context)
{
  Debug.Log("Fire Projectile action performed!");
  if (projectilePrefab != null && grabInteractable.selectingInteractor is XRBaseControllerInteractor controllerInteractor)
  {
    Transform firePoint = controllerInteractor.transform;
    GameObject projectile = Instantiate(projectilePrefab, firePoint.position, firePoint.rotation);
    Rigidbody rb = projectile.GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
    if (rb != null) rb.velocity = firePoint.forward * projectileSpeed;
    TriggerHaptic(controllerInteractor.xrController, 0.8f, 0.1f);
  }
}

private void TriggerHaptic(XRBaseController controller, float intensity, float duration)
{
  if (controller != null && controller.inputDevice.isValid)
  {
    controller.inputDevice.SendHapticImpulse(0, intensity, duration);
  }
}

screens.title: Haptic Feedback Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Haptics are tactile vibrations provided by controllers to simulate touch, impact, or continuous forces. In XR they serve two primary roles: reinforcing interactions and providing non-visual cues. Reinforcement examples include a light pulse when hovering over an interactable, a stronger jolt on impact, and a distinct pulse when firing a weapon. Non-visual cues include subtle guidance or confirmation when visual attention is elsewhere. The SendHapticImpulse A P I takes a channel index, an intensity value (commonly 0 to 1), and a duration in seconds. Use low intensity and short durations for hover and menu selection, and stronger, slightly longer pulses for impacts or weapon fire. A typical hazard is overuse: too many or too-strong vibrations cause discomfort or fatigue. Another misconception is assuming one intensity fits all events; instead, vary both intensity and duration to convey different meanings. Practically, design a small palette of haptic styles — hover, selection, impact — and reuse them consistently so users learn the tactile language. Finally, always check device validity before sending impulses to avoid runtime errors and keep haptics optional for accessibility. Haptic Feedback Fundamentals means use haptics to reinforce interactions and signal events; vary intensity and duration and avoid overuse to maintain comfort and clarity.. In practical terms, what haptics are and how they communicate events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Haptic Fundamentals
What is haptics?

Tactile feedback via controller vibrations

Haptic feedback conveys interaction meaning through intensity and duration. Use it to confirm selection, indicate impact, or provide continuous cues like carrying a heavy object.

Hover
Light, very short pulse (e.g., intensity 0.2, duration 0.05s).
Impact
Moderate pulse, slightly longer (e.g., intensity 0.7, duration 0.1s).
Avoid
High-intensity continuous vibration; causes discomfort and fatigue.
API
// SendHapticImpulse(channel, intensity, duration)
if (controller.inputDevice.isValid)
{
  controller.inputDevice.SendHapticImpulse(0, 0.7f, 0.1f);
}
Key Takeaway

Tune intensity and duration per event; use a small, consistent set of haptic styles for clarity and comfort.

Provide a TriggerHaptic method that accepts an XRBaseController or XRController reference along with intensity and duration, then check controller. inputDevice. isValid before calling SendHapticImpulse. This prevents attempts to vibrate an uninitialized or disconnected device. Use this helper in OnGrab and OnRelease event handlers on XRGrabInteractable: when the grab occurs, call TriggerHaptic with a light intensity; on release, call it with a stronger intensity. The chapter's CustomControllerActions and ThrowableObject scripts demonstrate this pattern, showing how to call TriggerHapticFeedback(0.5f, 0.2f) when firing a projectile, and different intensities for grab and release. Test your haptic patterns in Play Mode and iterate on intensity and duration values so they feel informative, not intrusive. This pattern makes your haptic code reusable and robust across controllers. Helper pattern
private void TriggerHaptic(XRBaseController controller, float intensity, float duration)
{
  if (controller != null && controller.inputDevice.isValid)
  {
    controller.inputDevice.SendHapticImpulse(0, intensity, duration);
  }
}
Use this helper in selectEntered and selectExited handlers to centralize haptic calls and to protect against invalid device references.
Usage examples
On grab
TriggerHaptic(controller, 0.3f, 0.1f) for a subtle confirmation when the object is selected.
On release
TriggerHaptic(controller, 0.5f, 0.15f) to emphasize the throw or drop event.
On fire
Trigger a short, strong pulse such as 0.8 intensity and 0.1s duration to match a projectile firing event.
Test values iteratively in Play Mode; start lower and increase intensity only if the tactile distinction is not clear.

screens.title: Designing Good Haptics and Avoiding Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Good haptic design follows clear principles: be subtle by default, vary intensity and duration to encode meaning, and keep haptics contextual so they match the event. Start with subtle pulses for hover and selection so feedback doesn’t dominate the experience. Use stronger pulses for impact or weapon fire but avoid continuous high-intensity vibrations. Vary both intensity and duration; a short high-intensity pulse feels different from a longer moderate pulse. Reuse a small palette of haptic styles so users learn the tactile language — for example: hover (short, low), select (short, medium), impact (short, high). Avoid overuse: too many pulses per second or prolonged vibration causes discomfort and can mask important events. Consider ergonomics and accessibility: rapid repeated impulses can cause strain. Also provide visual or auditory redundancy for critical cues so haptics augment rather than replace other senses. A common misconception is assuming stronger always equals better; in practice, stronger is more likely to be jarring. The practical step is to prototype a few patterns, try them in Play Mode, and iterate on intensity and length until interactions feel informative and comfortable.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Haptic Design
Principles
  • Subtle by default: favor short, low-intensity pulses for non-critical feedback.
  • Vary intensity and duration to convey different event types.
  • Contextual use: only vibrate when the feedback matches the user’s action.
  • Accessibility: avoid rapid repeated pulses and provide visual/auditory redundancy.
Key Takeaway

A small set of distinct haptic patterns, used consistently, communicates events effectively without causing fatigue.

Practical palette
Hover
Intensity 0.2, duration 0.05s.
Select
Intensity 0.4, duration 0.08s.
Impact
Intensity 0.7, duration 0.1–0.15s.
Iterate in Play Mode and test with different controllers to find comfortable defaults for your target hardware.

private void OnGrab(SelectEnterEventArgs args)
{

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how controllers make XR interactions feel direct and meaningful. We’ll start by configuring hand controllers so they can touch and grab objects, using the XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable components to make virtual objects respond like real ones. Next you’ll learn to wire controller buttons through Unity’s Input System so scripts can react to actions like firing a projectile. Then we’ll add haptics — short tactile impulses sent to the controller — so users feel collisions, grabs, and weapon fire. Along the way I’ll point out common setup mistakes, how to tune intensity and duration, and why thoughtful haptic design matters for comfort and clarity. By the end you should be able to set up a throwable object, trigger haptic pulses on grab and release, and design distinct vibration patterns that communicate different events. Think about a sphere that snaps to your hand, vibrates when you pick it up, and kicks when you fire it — that concrete behavior is our target. Ready to explore the key topics and build a simple throwable demo?

These objectives map to practical skills you will build. First, you will configure XR Direct Interactor and XR Grab Interactable so virtual objects respond to a user's hand presence and follow the controller when grabbed. That includes colliders, rigidbodies, and the Attach Transform concept. Second, you will implement button-press detection with Unity’s Input System and the XRI action-based controller model. You’ll learn how to create an action in an Input Action Asset, bind it to a controller control, and subscribe to events in C#. Third, you will integrate basic haptic feedback by calling SendHapticImpulse through the XR controller's input device and learn sensible defaults for intensity and duration. Finally, you will learn a pattern for wiring actions to gameplay code so grab, release, and custom actions like firing a projectile trigger both game logic and haptic responses. Each objective ties to the hands-on demo: a throwable sphere that vibrates on grab, release, and when you fire a projectile. Keep these goals in mind as we walk through setup, code, and haptic design.

These additional objectives focus on the technical checks and hands-on outcomes you will practice. First, you will learn to set and test Attach Transform on XRGrabInteractable so held objects align naturally with the controller; this avoids awkward snaps when grabbing. Second, you will master common troubleshooting steps: verify colliders are triggers, ensure appropriate Rigidbody settings, and confirm action maps are enabled. Third, you will wire haptics in your scripts using provided patterns so grab and release events call a single TriggerHaptic helper that checks device validity before sending impulses. Fourth, you will complete a hands-on throwable-object exercise: create a physics sphere, add XRGrabInteractable, configure a FireProjectile action, and trigger haptics on grab, release, and fire. Each skill is practical and testable in Play Mode, and practicing these checks prevents the two most frequent issues: missing rigidbodies and misaligned attach transforms. By the end you will have both a working demo and the debugging checklist to fix common failures.

Direct interaction models physical touch and grabbing in XR. The XR Direct Interactor is attached to a hand representation — typically a small trigger collider around the controller position plus a kinematic rigidbody — and it detects overlap with objects that have XRGrabInteractable. The XRGrabInteractable makes an object grabbable and controls how it follows the interactor. A key setting is Attach Transform: by placing an empty child at the desired holding point and assigning it, you define exactly where the object aligns with the hand. A concrete example: give each hand a sphere collider set as Is Trigger and a kinematic Rigidbody, add XR Direct Interactor to that hand, then add XRGrabInteractable to a Sphere in the scene. When you reach the collider into the sphere, the object becomes selectable and will follow the controller. A common misconception is thinking colliders alone are enough — without a properly configured Rigidbody on either the interactor or the interactable, physics-based detection or motion will fail. The takeaway is to treat the interactor, colliders, and rigidbodies as a small system: each must be present and correctly configured for natural grabbing behavior.

Configuring the hand controllers is a small sequence of precise steps that ensure reliable interaction. Start by locating your LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller as children of XR Origin. Add a Sphere Collider to each, and set Is Trigger so the collider does overlap checks rather than physical collisions. Then add a Rigidbody and mark it Is Kinematic on the hand object; this allows the interactor to participate in physics queries without being pushed by scene forces. Next, attach the XR Direct Interactor component to the same hand GameObject so the toolkit will treat the trigger collider as an interaction zone. For objects you want to pick up, add a Collider and a Rigidbody. Decide whether the object should be physics-driven when thrown — if so, leave Is Kinematic unchecked. Finally, add XRGrabInteractable to the object. A concrete example: for a throwable sphere, set its Rigidbody Is Kinematic to false so it reacts to forces, then assign XRGrabInteractable. Test in Play Mode: when the hand's trigger collider overlaps the sphere, it should become selectable. If not, check the Rigidbody presence and trigger setting. This step-by-step flow reduces common misconfiguration errors and produces predictable grab behavior.

XRGrabInteractable controls how an object is selected and how it moves when attached to a controller. A central property is Attach Transform: by default the object may attach at its root which often misaligns with natural grips. Create an empty GameObject as a child of the grabbable, position it where the virtual hand should hold the item, and assign that child to Attach Transform. This gives you precise control over rotation and offset so the object appears correctly held. Another important behavior is whether the object follows with physics or simply matches the controller transform. For physically realistic throws, leave the object's Rigidbody non-kinematic so physics apply when released; XRGrabInteractable supports picking up physics objects and applying release velocity. For static snapping behavior, mark the Rigidbody kinematic and the object will follow the interactor transform more directly. An example: to make a mug feel natural in the hand, create the grip attach point near the handle and adjust rotation so the mug's opening faces up. A common misconception is assuming Attach Transform only affects visuals — it actually defines the transform used by the interactor to position and rotate the object while held, and getting it wrong leads to awkward snaps and poor UX.

When a grab does not work or the object snaps strangely, two issues are usually responsible: collider/rigidbody misconfiguration and incorrect Attach Transform settings. First, check colliders. The hand collider should be set to Is Trigger. If it is not, it will generate physical collisions and can push objects away. Both the interactor and the interactable must have colliders that overlap. Second, verify Rigidbodies. The hand rigidbody is typically kinematic so it is not affected by physics forces, while the interactable's Rigidbody may be dynamic for throws. A missing Rigidbody on either side can prevent selection or cause jerky motion. Third, check Attach Transform: if the object snaps to an unexpected position, assign a child object positioned at the desired grip. Another frequent problem is disabled action maps or unbound actions preventing controller input events: when scripts look for an action that is not enabled, callbacks never fire. Finally, layering and collision matrix settings can hide overlaps. The practical fix is a short checklist: confirm trigger colliders, confirm rigidbodies, confirm Attach Transform, ensure action maps are enabled, and test in Play Mode. This focused troubleshooting flow resolves most common grabbing failures quickly.

Detecting button presses with the action-based model begins in the Input Action Asset. Open your XRI Default Input Actions or create a custom Input Action Asset. Inside the asset create or locate the action map for the hand you want to use, for example XRI RightHand. Add a new action named FireProjectile with Action Type set to Button and add a binding to the right-hand trigger control, such as the triggerPressed control for the XR controller. This abstract action can now be referenced by scripts without hardcoding device paths. In C#, you find the action map by name on the InputActionAsset and then FindAction to get the specific action. Enable the action map and subscribe to the action's performed event. A concrete example is adding a FireProjectile action bound to the right trigger and in Start() enabling the map and subscribing to performed. A common pitfall is forgetting to enable the action map, which results in callbacks never firing. Another is using a wrong action path; always test bindings in Play Mode. The result is a clean, decoupled way to respond to controller buttons across devices and form factors.

Once your Input Action Asset contains the desired action, your script should locate the action map and action, enable the map, and then subscribe to the action events. The example in the lesson shows finding the XRI RightHand action map and then calling FindAction to get FireProjectile. After enabling the map, subscribe to performed to run your logic when the button is pressed. In the handler you can instantiate gameplay objects such as a projectile and then call a haptic helper to provide tactile feedback. Importantly, unsubscribe in OnDestroy to avoid dangling callbacks. Also, check that the XRController reference used to send haptics is assigned and that its inputDevice is valid before calling SendHapticImpulse. A concrete example: call TriggerHapticFeedback(0.5f, 0.2f) after instantiating a projectile. A common error is not checking controller. inputDevice. isValid which will cause SendHapticImpulse to silently do nothing; always guard your haptic call with a validity check. The end result is a clean wiring where button presses spawn projectiles and immediately send a haptic pulse so the player receives both visual and tactile confirmation. Wiring Input Actions to Controller Scripts means enable the action map, subscribe to performed, perform gameplay logic, and call a guarded haptic helper that checks device validity.. Haptics are tactile vibrations provided by controllers to simulate touch, impact, or continuous forces. In XR they serve two primary roles: reinforcing interactions and providing non-visual cues. Reinforcement examples include a light pulse when hovering over an interactable, a stronger jolt on impact, and a distinct pulse when firing a weapon. Non-visual cues include subtle guidance or confirmation when visual attention is elsewhere. The SendHapticImpulse A P I takes a channel index, an intensity value (commonly 0 to 1), and a duration in seconds. Use low intensity and short durations for hover and menu selection, and stronger, slightly longer pulses for impacts or weapon fire. A typical hazard is overuse: too many or too-strong vibrations cause discomfort or fatigue. Another misconception is assuming one intensity fits all events; instead, vary both intensity and duration to convey different meanings. Practically, design a small palette of haptic styles — hover, selection, impact — and reuse them consistently so users learn the tactile language. Finally, always check device validity before sending impulses to avoid runtime errors and keep haptics optional for accessibility. Good haptic design follows clear principles: be subtle by default, vary intensity and duration to encode meaning, and keep haptics contextual so they match the event. Start with subtle pulses for hover and selection so feedback doesn’t dominate the experience. Use stronger pulses for impact or weapon fire but avoid continuous high-intensity vibrations. Vary both intensity and duration; a short high-intensity pulse feels different from a longer moderate pulse. Reuse a small palette of haptic styles so users learn the tactile language — for example: hover (short, low), select (short, medium), impact (short, high). Avoid overuse: too many pulses per second or prolonged vibration causes discomfort and can mask important events. Consider ergonomics and accessibility: rapid repeated impulses can cause strain. Also provide visual or auditory redundancy for critical cues so haptics augment rather than replace other senses. A common misconception is assuming stronger always equals better; in practice, stronger is more likely to be jarring. The practical step is to prototype a few patterns, try them in Play Mode, and iterate on intensity and length until interactions feel informative and comfortable.
